question_or_heading: Where the income statement starts
option_a: Revenue — also called sales or turnover — is the total amount a company earned from its core business activities before subtracting any costs. It sits at the very top of the income statement.

question_or_heading: Recognized when earned, not when paid
option_a: Revenue is typically recorded when a good or service is delivered, not necessarily when cash actually changes hands — a sale on credit still counts as revenue immediately.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Revenue is the total value of goods or services delivered in a period, recorded when earned — not necessarily when cash is received.

question_or_heading: A company delivers ₹5,00,000 worth of goods to a customer in March, but the customer only pays in May. When is this revenue typically recorded?
option_a: In May, when cash is received
option_b: In March, when the goods were delivered
option_c: Split evenly between March and May
option_d: Never, until fully paid
hint: Is revenue recognized on delivery, or on payment?
explanation: Revenue is generally recognized when it's earned — when the goods are delivered — not when cash actually arrives.

question_or_heading: Which of these best describes 'revenue' on an income statement?
option_a: Profit after all expenses
option_b: The total amount earned from core business activities, before any costs are subtracted
option_c: Cash currently in the bank
option_d: The value of unsold inventory
hint: Is revenue a starting point or an ending result on the income statement?
explanation: Revenue is the starting 'top line' — the full amount earned from the business, before a single expense is subtracted.

question_or_heading: Revenue and cash received are always exactly the same number in the same period.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: What did the intro cards say about credit sales?
explanation: Revenue can be recognized before cash is actually collected — a credit sale counts as revenue right away, even though the cash shows up later.

question_or_heading: Why is revenue called the 'top line'?
option_a: Because it's always the largest number on any financial statement
option_b: Because it's the first line item on the income statement, before any costs are deducted
option_c: Because it's the least important figure
option_d: Because it only applies to top-performing companies
hint: Where does it physically sit on the page, relative to every deduction that follows?
explanation: It sits at the very top of the income statement — every other line represents a cost being subtracted from it, working down toward profit.

question_or_heading: A software company signs a 12-month subscription contract worth ₹12,00,000, paid upfront in January. How is this revenue typically recognized?
option_a: All ₹12,00,000 in January, since that's when cash arrived
option_b: Spread across the 12 months as the service is actually delivered, roughly ₹1,00,000 per month
option_c: Never recognized as revenue
option_d: Only recognized at the end of the 12 months
hint: Is the whole service delivered on day one, or spread over the year?
explanation: Since the service is delivered gradually over 12 months, revenue is typically recognized as it's earned each month — not dumped entirely into the month cash was collected.

lesson_title: Cost of Goods Sold & Gross Profit
question_or_heading: COGS: the direct cost of what was sold
option_a: Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) captures the direct costs of producing or acquiring whatever the company sold — raw materials, direct labor, manufacturing costs.

lesson_title: Cost of Goods Sold & Gross Profit
question_or_heading: Gross profit is the first real margin
option_a: Gross Profit = Revenue − COGS. It shows how much is left after covering the direct cost of the product itself, before any overhead, marketing, or admin costs.

lesson_title: Cost of Goods Sold & Gross Profit
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Gross Profit = Revenue − Cost of Goods Sold — the profit left after covering only the direct cost of what was sold.

lesson_title: Cost of Goods Sold & Gross Profit
question_or_heading: A company has ₹1,00,00,000 in revenue and ₹60,00,000 in COGS. What is its gross profit?
hint: Gross Profit = Revenue − COGS.
explanation: ₹1,00,00,000 − ₹60,00,000 = ₹40,00,000 — what's left after covering the direct cost of producing what was sold.

lesson_title: Cost of Goods Sold & Gross Profit
question_or_heading: Which of these would typically be included in COGS for a furniture manufacturer?
option_a: The CEO's salary
option_b: Wood and direct factory labor used to build the furniture sold
option_c: National advertising campaign costs
option_d: Office rent for headquarters
hint: Which cost is directly tied to physically producing the units sold?
explanation: Raw materials and direct production labor are classic COGS — costs directly tied to making what was sold, unlike overhead like admin salaries or marketing.

lesson_title: Cost of Goods Sold & Gross Profit
question_or_heading: Gross profit already accounts for marketing, admin, and overhead costs.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: What's subtracted to get gross profit — just COGS, or COGS plus everything else too?
explanation: Gross profit only subtracts COGS. Marketing, admin, and overhead come out later, on the way to operating income.

lesson_title: Cost of Goods Sold & Gross Profit
question_or_heading: A retailer's gross profit margin (gross profit ÷ revenue) is 40%. What does this tell you?
option_a: 40% of revenue is pure net profit
option_b: For every ₹100 of sales, ₹40 remains after covering the direct cost of the goods sold
option_c: The company spends 40% of revenue on marketing
option_d: The company has 40% market share
hint: Gross margin isolates just one layer of cost — which one?
explanation: A 40% gross margin means ₹40 of every ₹100 in sales survives after covering just the direct product cost — before any other expenses are even considered.

lesson_title: Cost of Goods Sold & Gross Profit
question_or_heading: Why might comparing gross margins across two very different industries (say, software vs. heavy manufacturing) be misleading?
option_a: Gross margins are identical across all industries by law
option_b: Different industries have structurally different cost bases — software has very low COGS while manufacturing typically has much higher COGS relative to revenue
option_c: Gross margin only applies to manufacturing companies
option_d: There's no meaningful difference between industries
hint: Does a software company's 'cost of goods sold' look anything like a factory's?
explanation: Structural differences in COGS between industries (software's low direct costs versus manufacturing's heavy material and labor costs) make cross-industry gross margin comparisons far less meaningful than comparisons within the same industry.

question_or_heading: Running the business, beyond the product itself
option_a: Operating expenses cover the costs of running the business that aren't directly tied to producing the product — selling, general, and administrative expenses (SG&A), R&D, marketing.

question_or_heading: Below gross profit, above operating income
option_a: Operating expenses are subtracted from gross profit to arrive at operating income — capturing the full cost of actually running the business day to day.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Operating expenses are the costs of running the business beyond direct production — like SG&A, marketing, and R&D — subtracted from gross profit.

question_or_heading: Which of these is a classic operating expense, rather than part of COGS?
option_a: Raw materials used in manufacturing
option_b: The marketing team's salaries and ad spend
option_c: Direct factory labor
option_d: Shipping costs to move raw materials to the factory
hint: Which of these is unrelated to directly producing the physical product?
explanation: Marketing costs support selling the product but aren't part of physically making it — a textbook operating expense (SG&A), distinct from COGS.

question_or_heading: A pharmaceutical company spends heavily on R&D to develop new drugs. Where does this cost typically appear on the income statement?
option_a: As part of COGS
option_b: As an operating expense, since it's part of running and growing the business, not direct production of already-sold goods
option_c: It never appears on the income statement
option_d: As a reduction to revenue
hint: Is R&D spend a direct cost of goods already sold, or a broader cost of operating and growing the business?
explanation: R&D is a classic operating expense — critical to the business, but not a direct cost of goods already sold, so it sits below gross profit, not inside COGS.

question_or_heading: Operating expenses are subtracted from revenue directly, skipping the gross profit calculation entirely.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: What's the actual sequence: Revenue → COGS → Gross Profit → then what?
explanation: Operating expenses are subtracted from gross profit (which itself came from Revenue minus COGS) — not straight from revenue.

question_or_heading: A company cuts its marketing budget sharply to boost short-term profit. What's a reasonable long-term concern with this move?
option_a: There's no possible downside to cutting marketing
option_b: Reduced marketing could slow future revenue growth, even though it boosts current-period operating income
option_c: Marketing spend never affects revenue
option_d: Cutting marketing always increases revenue
hint: What might marketing spend be buying the company, beyond this period's expenses?
explanation: While cutting marketing lifts short-term operating income, it can undercut future customer acquisition and revenue growth — a classic short-term-versus-long-term trade-off analysts watch for.

question_or_heading: Why do analysts often examine operating expenses as a PERCENTAGE of revenue, rather than just the raw rupee amount?
option_a: Percentages are always more accurate than raw numbers
option_b: It helps track efficiency and spot trends — whether costs are growing faster or slower than the business itself, regardless of scale
option_c: Raw rupee amounts are illegal to disclose
option_d: Percentages eliminate the need for any other financial analysis
hint: What does tracking a cost as a share of revenue reveal that the raw number alone doesn't?
explanation: Expressing operating expenses as a percentage of revenue reveals whether spending is scaling in line with the business, growing faster (a red flag), or shrinking (improving efficiency) — insight the raw number alone doesn't give.

question_or_heading: The profit from core operations
option_a: Operating Income — also called EBIT (Earnings Before Interest and Taxes) — measures profit purely from the core business, before financing costs (interest) and tax effects muddy the picture.

question_or_heading: Why EBIT is useful for comparisons
option_a: Because it excludes interest and taxes, EBIT lets you compare the core operating performance of companies with very different debt levels or tax situations more fairly.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Operating Income (EBIT) = Gross Profit − Operating Expenses — profit from the core business, before interest and taxes.

question_or_heading: A company has gross profit of ₹40,00,000 and operating expenses of ₹25,00,000. What is its operating income (EBIT)?
hint: EBIT = Gross Profit − Operating Expenses.
explanation: ₹40,00,000 − ₹25,00,000 = ₹15,00,000 — the profit generated purely by core operations, before interest and taxes are considered.

question_or_heading: Why might an analyst prefer comparing two companies using EBIT rather than net income, if one company has much more debt than the other?
option_a: EBIT and net income are always identical
option_b: EBIT excludes interest expense, so it isolates operating performance without letting differing debt loads distort the comparison
option_c: Net income is always the better metric in every situation
option_d: EBIT only applies to companies with zero debt
hint: Which metric strips out the effect of how the company happens to be financed?
explanation: Stripping out interest (and taxes) lets EBIT compare the underlying businesses on a more level footing, regardless of how much debt each happens to carry.

question_or_heading: EBIT stands for 'Earnings Before Interest and Taxes.'
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Sound out the acronym letter by letter.
explanation: EBIT is literally an acronym for Earnings Before Interest and Taxes — profit measured before those two items are subtracted.

question_or_heading: Two companies have identical EBIT, but Company A has much more debt (and therefore higher interest expense) than Company B. What would you expect regarding their net income?
option_a: Both will have identical net income
option_b: Company A's net income will likely be lower, since more interest expense gets subtracted after EBIT
option_c: Company B's net income will definitely be lower
option_d: Debt has no effect on net income
hint: What gets subtracted from EBIT to eventually reach net income, and how does debt level affect that?
explanation: Since interest expense gets subtracted after EBIT, and Company A carries more debt (more interest), its net income would typically end up lower than Company B's despite identical operating performance.

question_or_heading: Why is EBIT often described as a measure of a company's 'core' business performance?
option_a: Because it includes every possible expense a company has
option_b: Because it captures profit purely from operations, excluding financing decisions (interest) and tax jurisdiction effects (taxes)
option_c: Because 'core' companies are a specific legal category
option_d: Because it only applies to the company's headquarters location
hint: What two things does EBIT deliberately exclude, and why does that make it feel more 'core'?
explanation: By deliberately excluding interest (a financing choice) and taxes (often driven by jurisdiction and policy, not operations), EBIT isolates something closer to the pure operating engine of the business.

question_or_heading: Interest: the cost of borrowed money
option_a: Interest expense reflects what a company pays on its debt. It's subtracted after EBIT, since it depends on financing choices, not core operating performance.

question_or_heading: Taxes come next
option_a: After interest, taxes owed to the government are subtracted, based on the applicable tax rate and taxable income — arriving finally at net income, the true bottom line.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: EBIT minus interest expense minus taxes equals net income — financing costs and government's share, both subtracted after core operating profit.

question_or_heading: A company has EBIT of ₹20,00,000, interest expense of ₹4,00,000, and a tax rate of 25% applied to the remaining amount. What is its approximate net income?
hint: First subtract interest, then apply the tax rate to what's left, then subtract that tax.

question_or_heading: Why is interest expense subtracted AFTER operating income (EBIT), rather than being included in operating expenses?
option_a: It's an arbitrary accounting choice with no real logic
option_b: Interest reflects financing decisions (how much debt the company chose to take on), separate from how the core business actually operates
option_c: Interest is always zero for most companies
option_d: Operating expenses and interest are the exact same thing
hint: What category of decision does interest expense reflect — operating the business, or financing it?
explanation: Interest reflects a financing decision — how much debt the company chose to carry — which is deliberately kept separate from the operating performance captured in EBIT.

question_or_heading: Net income is calculated before subtracting both interest and taxes.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Where do interest and taxes fall in the sequence toward net income — before it, or as part of getting to it?
explanation: Net income is exactly what's left AFTER both interest and taxes are subtracted from EBIT — it's the true final bottom line, not a figure that precedes those deductions.

question_or_heading: Two companies have identical EBIT, but Company X operates in a country with a much higher corporate tax rate than Company Y. All else equal, what would you expect?
option_a: Both will have identical net income
option_b: Company X's net income will likely be lower, due to the higher tax bite on the same pre-tax income
option_c: Company Y's EBIT will be different as a result
option_d: Tax rates never affect net income
hint: Which company loses more of its pre-tax income to taxes?
explanation: A higher tax rate takes a bigger bite out of the same pre-tax income, leaving Company X with lower net income despite identical operating performance to Company Y.

question_or_heading: Why do analysts sometimes look at both EBIT and net income when evaluating a company, rather than just net income alone?
option_a: Net income is always a completely useless number
option_b: EBIT isolates operating performance, while net income reflects the full picture including financing and tax effects — together they tell a fuller story
option_c: EBIT and net income are always exactly equal, so it doesn't matter which is used
option_d: Only net income is ever relevant for any analysis
hint: What does each metric add that the other one doesn't capture on its own?
explanation: Looking at both lets an analyst separate how well the core business is performing (EBIT) from how financing and tax choices affect the final bottom line (net income) — a more complete picture than either alone.

question_or_heading: The final number
option_a: Net income is what's left after every single expense — COGS, operating expenses, interest, taxes — has been subtracted from revenue. It's the company's total profit for the period.

question_or_heading: Where net income goes
option_a: Net income either gets paid out to shareholders as dividends, or kept and reinvested in the business, adding to retained earnings on the balance sheet.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Net income is the final bottom-line profit after every expense — COGS, operating costs, interest, and taxes — has been subtracted from revenue.

question_or_heading: Which sequence correctly shows the flow from revenue down to net income?
option_a: Revenue → Net Income → COGS → Taxes
option_b: Revenue → COGS → Gross Profit → Operating Expenses → Operating Income (EBIT) → Interest → Taxes → Net Income
option_c: Net Income → Revenue → Expenses
option_d: Revenue → Taxes → Interest → COGS → Net Income
hint: Recall the order you've built up across this whole unit, lesson by lesson.
explanation: This is the full waterfall this unit has built lesson by lesson: revenue at the top, each cost layer subtracted in sequence, landing on net income at the very bottom.

question_or_heading: A company's net income for the year is ₹50,00,000. What are the two main things this profit can be used for?
option_a: Only ever paid out as dividends
option_b: Paid out to shareholders as dividends, and/or retained and reinvested in the business (adding to retained earnings)
option_c: It must be spent entirely on marketing
option_d: It legally has to be donated to charity
hint: Recall the balance sheet unit's discussion of retained earnings — where does profit that isn't paid out go?
explanation: Net income splits between what's distributed to shareholders as dividends and what's kept in the business, flowing into retained earnings on the balance sheet.

question_or_heading: Net income is also commonly referred to as the 'bottom line.'
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Where does it physically sit on the income statement, relative to the 'top line' (revenue)?
explanation: Net income sits at the very bottom of the income statement, after every deduction — which is exactly why it's colloquially called 'the bottom line.'

question_or_heading: A company reports strong revenue growth but declining net income. What does this combination most directly suggest?
option_a: The company's costs are growing faster than its revenue, squeezing profitability despite top-line growth
option_b: Revenue and net income always move in the same direction, so this can't happen
option_c: The company must be committing fraud
option_d: Net income is unrelated to revenue
hint: If the top line is growing but the bottom line is shrinking, what must be happening in between?
explanation: Growing revenue but shrinking net income points squarely at costs — somewhere between COGS, operating expenses, interest, or taxes — growing even faster than the top line.

question_or_heading: Why might two companies with identical net income still be viewed very differently by investors?
option_a: Identical net income means they must be identical companies in every way
option_b: The quality and composition of that net income can differ — driven by core operations vs. one-time gains, or backed by strong cash flow vs. weak cash flow
option_c: Net income is the only number investors ever look at
option_d: There's no way to distinguish between two companies with the same net income
hint: Does the SIZE of net income tell you anything about where it came from, or how sustainable it is?
explanation: Net income alone doesn't reveal its source or sustainability — a company earning it from steady core operations looks very different from one hitting the same number via a one-time asset sale, even though the reported figure matches.

question_or_heading: Spreading net income across shares
option_a: Earnings Per Share (EPS) = Net Income ÷ Number of Shares Outstanding. It translates total company profit into a per-share figure investors can compare more intuitively.

question_or_heading: Why EPS alone can mislead
option_a: A company can boost EPS just by buying back and cancelling shares, even if total net income doesn't grow at all — so EPS growth isn't automatically the same as genuine business growth.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: EPS = Net Income ÷ Shares Outstanding — a per-share slice of total profit, useful but sensitive to share count changes, not just underlying profit growth.

question_or_heading: A company has net income of ₹10,00,00,000 and 50,00,000 shares outstanding. What is its EPS?
hint: EPS = Net Income ÷ Shares Outstanding.
explanation: ₹10,00,00,000 ÷ 50,00,000 = ₹200 per share — that's the slice of total profit attributable to each individual share.

question_or_heading: A company's net income stays flat year over year, but it buys back and cancels 20% of its outstanding shares. What happens to EPS?
option_a: EPS stays exactly the same
option_b: EPS rises, purely because the same profit is now divided among fewer shares
option_c: EPS falls sharply
option_d: EPS becomes impossible to calculate
hint: Same numerator, smaller denominator — what happens to the ratio?
explanation: With the same net income divided across fewer shares, EPS rises mechanically — even though the underlying business didn't actually grow its profit at all.

question_or_heading: Rising EPS always means a company's underlying business is genuinely growing more profitable.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Recall the share buyback example — can EPS rise without any real growth in net income?
explanation: As the buyback example shows, EPS can rise purely from a shrinking share count, with zero real growth in the underlying business — so rising EPS alone isn't proof of genuine improvement.

question_or_heading: Why do investors commonly use EPS to compare companies, rather than raw net income alone?
option_a: Raw net income is always more useful and EPS should be ignored
option_b: EPS adjusts for the number of shares outstanding, making it easier to judge and compare profit on a per-share, per-investor basis
option_c: EPS and net income are always identical numbers
option_d: EPS only applies to companies that pay dividends
hint: What problem does dividing by share count solve when comparing companies of different sizes?
explanation: Since companies have wildly different numbers of shares outstanding, raw net income alone doesn't tell an individual shareholder much — EPS translates total profit into a comparable per-share figure.

question_or_heading: An analyst sees a company's EPS grew 15% this year. What's a sensible next step before concluding the business is genuinely performing better?
option_a: Immediately assume the business grew 15% and stop analyzing
option_b: Check whether that EPS growth came mainly from real net income growth, or partly/mostly from a shrinking share count due to buybacks
option_c: EPS growth never needs further investigation
option_d: Assume the company is committing accounting fraud
hint: What two very different explanations could produce the same EPS growth number?
explanation: Since EPS growth can come from genuine profit growth OR a shrinking share count (or some mix of both), a careful analyst checks the source before concluding the underlying business is truly performing better.

question_or_heading: Not every expense repeats every year
option_a: Some costs — a lawsuit settlement, a factory closure charge, a one-time asset write-down — happen once and aren't expected to recur, unlike ongoing costs like salaries or rent.

question_or_heading: Why they distort a single year's numbers
option_a: A big one-time charge can make an otherwise healthy year's net income look much worse than the business's true ongoing earning power — and the reverse is true for one-time gains.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: One-time or non-recurring items are unusual, unlikely-to-repeat charges or gains that can distort a single period's reported profit relative to the business's ongoing earning power.

question_or_heading: A company reports a big drop in net income this year, driven mostly by a one-time ₹15,00,000 lawsuit settlement charge. How should an analyst likely treat this when judging the business's ongoing health?
option_a: Assume the business's true earning power has permanently dropped by that same amount
option_b: Recognize it as a one-time item and look at what net income would have been without it, to judge the underlying ongoing business separately
option_c: Ignore net income entirely from now on
option_d: Assume the lawsuit will recur every year going forward
hint: Is a lawsuit settlement charge something expected to repeat annually, or a one-off event?
explanation: Since a one-time lawsuit settlement isn't part of the business's normal, repeating cost structure, a careful analyst adjusts for it to judge the company's true, ongoing earning power separately.

question_or_heading: Which of these would typically be classified as a recurring (not one-time) expense?
option_a: A factory closure charge taken once
option_b: Employee salaries, paid every single period as part of normal operations
option_c: A one-off asset write-down
option_d: A rare legal settlement
hint: Which of these happens every period as part of just running the business?
explanation: Salaries are a routine, ongoing cost of operating the business — the opposite of a one-time, non-recurring item.

question_or_heading: A company that highlights 'adjusted' earnings, excluding one-time items, every single year without exception, deserves extra scrutiny.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: If 'unusual' items show up every single year, are they really unusual?
explanation: If supposedly non-recurring charges show up year after year, they start to look like a normal, recurring part of the business — and heavy reliance on 'adjusted' figures to mask that is worth extra scrutiny.

question_or_heading: Why might a company's management prefer to emphasize 'adjusted' earnings (excluding one-time items) over standard net income when presenting results?
option_a: Adjusted earnings are always required by accounting regulators
option_b: Adjusted figures, by excluding unflattering one-time charges, can sometimes present a rosier picture of performance than standard net income
option_c: Adjusted earnings and net income are always identical
option_d: Standard net income is illegal to disclose
hint: Whose interest might be served by a metric that strips out the year's worst charges?
explanation: Excluding unflattering one-time charges can make performance look better than the standard net income figure — which is exactly why analysts treat heavily 'adjusted' metrics with some healthy skepticism.

question_or_heading: An analyst is comparing a company's profitability across five years, and one of those years included a large one-time gain from selling an unused property. What's the most sensible approach?
option_a: Include the one-time gain identically to every other year without comment
option_b: Note the one-time gain separately and consider looking at that year's results both with and without it, to see the underlying trend clearly
option_c: Delete that year from the analysis entirely
option_d: Assume such gains happen every year going forward
hint: How can you see the real underlying trend while still being honest about what actually happened that year?
explanation: Flagging the one-time gain and viewing results both with and without it lets the analyst see the genuine underlying trend, without either hiding what happened or letting a one-off event distort the full five-year picture.

question_or_heading: Margins standardize profitability
option_a: A margin expresses a profit figure as a percentage of revenue — gross margin, operating margin, net margin — making it possible to compare companies of very different sizes fairly.

question_or_heading: Each margin tells a different part of the story
option_a: Gross margin shows product-level profitability. Operating margin adds in the cost of running the business. Net margin captures everything, including financing and taxes.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: A margin is a profit figure divided by revenue — turning rupee amounts into comparable percentages, at each stage of the income statement.

question_or_heading: Company A earns ₹10,00,000 net income on ₹1,00,00,000 revenue. Company B earns ₹50,00,000 net income on ₹10,00,00,000 revenue. Which has the higher net margin?
option_a: Company A (10%) vs Company B (5%) — Company A
option_b: Company B, since it has higher absolute profit
option_c: They're identical
option_d: Not enough information to compare
hint: Calculate net income ÷ revenue for each, as a percentage.
explanation: Company A: ₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,00,000 = 10%. Company B: ₹50,00,000 ÷ ₹10,00,00,000 = 5%. Despite Company B's much larger absolute profit, Company A is more profitable per rupee of sales.

question_or_heading: Which margin captures the FULL picture, including COGS, operating expenses, interest, and taxes?
option_a: Gross margin
option_b: Operating margin
option_c: Net margin
option_d: None of them include taxes
hint: Which margin sits at the very bottom of the income statement, after every deduction?
explanation: Net margin (net income ÷ revenue) is the only one of the three that reflects every single deduction, all the way down to the final bottom line.

question_or_heading: A company with a higher absolute net income figure always has a higher net margin than a company with a smaller absolute net income figure.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does size of profit alone determine the percentage margin, without knowing revenue too?
explanation: As the earlier example showed, a smaller absolute profit can still represent a higher margin if it comes from proportionally less revenue — margin depends on the ratio, not just the raw profit size.

question_or_heading: Why are margins generally more useful than raw profit figures when comparing a small company to a much larger one?
option_a: Raw profit figures are always more meaningful for any comparison
option_b: Margins express profitability as a percentage, letting you compare efficiency fairly regardless of the two companies' very different scales
option_c: Margins only apply to companies of similar size
option_d: There's no real difference between margins and raw figures
hint: What problem does expressing profit as a percentage of revenue solve when sizes differ hugely?
explanation: Turning profit into a percentage of revenue neutralizes the effect of sheer size, letting you compare how efficiently each company converts sales into profit — regardless of one being much bigger than the other.

question_or_heading: A company's gross margin stays steady at 50% for years, but its net margin steadily declines over the same period. What does this combination suggest?
option_a: Product-level profitability (gross margin) is stable, but rising costs further down the income statement — operating expenses, interest, or taxes — are eating into the bottom line
option_b: The company's core product economics are deteriorating
option_c: Gross margin and net margin are always identical
option_d: This combination is mathematically impossible
hint: If gross margin is stable but net margin isn't, where must the changing cost pressure be coming from — the product itself, or something further down the statement?
explanation: Since gross margin (which reflects only product-level cost) is stable, the declining net margin points to rising costs further down the statement — operating expenses, interest, or taxes eating progressively more into the bottom line.

lesson_title: Capstone: Reading a Real Income Statement
question_or_heading: Walk the waterfall
option_a: Reading an income statement well means following the waterfall from revenue down to net income, checking each margin along the way, and asking what's driving the changes at each step.

lesson_title: Capstone: Reading a Real Income Statement
question_or_heading: Context beats a single number
option_a: No single line item tells the whole story — comparing this year to last year, and comparing margins to peers, is what turns raw numbers into real insight.

lesson_title: Capstone: Reading a Real Income Statement
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Reading an income statement well means tracing revenue down to net income step by step, checking each margin, and comparing across time and to peers.

question_or_heading: A company's revenue grew 20% year over year, but its operating margin fell from 25% to 15%. What's the most sensible interpretation?
option_a: The company is definitely failing and about to go bankrupt
option_b: Revenue is growing, but operating costs are growing even faster relative to sales — worth investigating which cost category is driving that
option_c: This combination is mathematically impossible
option_d: Margins are irrelevant if revenue is growing
hint: If the top line grew but a margin fell, what does that say about the growth rate of costs relative to revenue?
explanation: Growing revenue alongside a shrinking operating margin means operating costs grew even faster than sales — a pattern worth digging into, using the operating expenses lesson's tools, before drawing conclusions.

lesson_title: Capstone: Reading a Real Income Statement
question_or_heading: An analyst notices a company's net margin jumped sharply in one year, driven almost entirely by a one-time gain on selling a subsidiary. How should this be treated when assessing the company's underlying trend?
option_a: Treated identically to organic, recurring profit growth
option_b: Flagged as a one-time item and excluded when judging the ongoing, sustainable earning power of the business
option_c: Ignored entirely, along with the whole income statement
option_d: Assumed to repeat every year from now on
hint: Recall the one-time items lesson — how should a non-recurring gain be treated in trend analysis?
explanation: Consistent with the earlier lesson on one-time items, a one-off gain like a subsidiary sale should be flagged and set aside when judging the company's genuine, ongoing profitability trend.

lesson_title: Capstone: Reading a Real Income Statement
question_or_heading: Comparing a company's margins only to its own past performance, without ever comparing to industry peers, gives a complete picture of its financial health.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does 'improving compared to last year' automatically mean 'good compared to the industry'?
explanation: A company can be improving over time yet still lag far behind its peers — or vice versa. Comparing to peers, not just your own history, is an important complementary check.

lesson_title: Capstone: Reading a Real Income Statement
question_or_heading: Putting this whole unit together — revenue, COGS, gross profit, operating expenses, EBIT, interest, taxes, net income, EPS, margins — what's the single biggest skill this builds?
option_a: Memorizing every line item's exact legal definition
option_b: The ability to trace how a rupee of revenue transforms, step by step, into a rupee of final profit — and to spot where that transformation is unusually strong or weak
option_c: The ability to predict stock prices with certainty
option_d: None of these lessons connect to each other
hint: What's the connecting thread across every lesson in this unit, from revenue down to margins?
explanation: This whole unit builds toward exactly that: the ability to trace revenue's journey down to net income step by step, and to spot precisely where in that journey a company is unusually strong, weak, or worth a closer look.

lesson_title: Capstone: Reading a Real Income Statement
question_or_heading: You're handed an income statement showing rising revenue, stable gross margin, but declining EPS. Based on this unit, what would you check first?
option_a: Nothing further — the numbers speak entirely for themselves
option_b: Whether share count has grown (diluting EPS) or whether costs below the gross profit line (operating expenses, interest, taxes) have risen faster than revenue
option_c: Assume this is definitely fraud
option_d: Ignore EPS entirely, since it's a meaningless metric
hint: Recall the EPS lesson — what TWO different things could explain declining EPS even with stable gross margin?
explanation: Since stable gross margin rules out product-level cost issues, declining EPS despite rising revenue points to either a growing share count (diluting the per-share slice) or rising costs further down the statement — exactly the two threads this unit equipped you to check.
